passages.title: Solomon is anointed during a succession dispute
passages.summary: Adonijah gathers supporters at En Rogel. Bathsheba and Nathan approach David, who orders Solomon’s anointing at Gihon. Succession depends on public recognition and access to the aging king. Abishag serves David, but the text denies sexual relations.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: Original study reflection: examine who has a voice when leaders transfer authority.

passages.title: David dies and Solomon consolidates power
passages.summary: David gives final instructions. Solomon removes Abiathar and orders the deaths of Adonijah, Joab, and Shimei. The royal transition combines covenant advice, political threats, and executions. The guide does not infer every private motive behind the request for Abishag.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: Original study reflection: distinguish a ruler’s claim of justice from proof that every action is justified.

passages.title: Solomon asks for wisdom and judges a dispute
passages.summary: At Gibeon, Solomon asks for an understanding heart. In Jerusalem, two women dispute the identity of a living infant. The threatened division of the child exposes a difference between the women’s responses. It is a judgment story, not a recommended parenting test.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me encourages seeking discernment between right and wrong.

passages.title: Officials, provisions, and wisdom
passages.summary: The chapter lists officials, regional suppliers, royal provisions, and Solomon’s reputation for wisdom. A prosperous court requires workers, food, and administration. Its numerical claims are preserved as textual claims, not independently measured totals.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: Original study reflection: identify the labor and resources behind a description of prosperity.

passages.title: Hiram supplies timber for the temple
passages.summary: Solomon and Hiram arrange timber and food exchanges. Adoniram supervises a labor levy, while builders prepare stone and wood. International cooperation and compelled labor support construction. The guide keeps workers visible alongside the royal achievement.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: Original study reflection: consider how sacred projects affect the people who build them.

passages.title: The temple is built
passages.summary: The account describes the temple’s rooms, wooden carvings, gold covering, and cherubim. God’s promise also requires faithful conduct. The building description is a literary account. The map marks Jerusalem without claiming a verified floor plan or exact surviving foundation.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me invites reflection on sacred space and temple symbols.

passages.title: Royal buildings and bronze furnishings
passages.summary: Solomon’s palace buildings are described. Hiram the bronze worker makes pillars, the sea, movable stands, and other vessels. Hiram the artisan is distinct from the king of Tyre. The chapter describes craft knowledge and materials alongside royal buildings.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: The older manual connects the bronze sea with baptism. This is an LDS interpretation, not archaeological proof.

passages.title: The ark enters the temple and Solomon prays
passages.summary: The ark is brought into the sanctuary. Solomon prays about justice, forgiveness, drought, foreigners, war, and exile. The prayer says heaven cannot contain God. It joins a particular sacred house with concern for people beyond Israel.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me connects the dedication prayer with temple covenants and walking in God’s ways.

passages.title: Promises, warnings, labor, and trade
passages.summary: God answers Solomon with a promise and warning. The chapter describes towns, building projects, labor, and ships sailing toward Ophir. Sacred status does not remove accountability. Ophir’s location is disputed, so the guide does not invent a destination or sea route.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies God’s promises and the responsibility to keep covenants.

passages.title: The queen of Sheba visits
passages.summary: The queen tests Solomon with questions and sees the court. Gifts, trade, gold, horses, and royal wealth follow. The narrative presents international reputation and abundance. The queen is unnamed, and no exact journey or independent inventory is established here.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: Original study reflection: compare admiration for wealth with the responsibilities of a ruler.

passages.title: Solomon turns away and adversaries rise
passages.summary: Solomon supports other gods. Hadad and Rezon become adversaries. Ahijah promises Jeroboam a kingdom, and Solomon later dies. The account holds Solomon responsible for his worship. It also recalls displaced people and rival powers, rather than only court prosperity.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me asks readers to examine influences that turn their hearts from God.

passages.title: Rehoboam rejects the petition and the kingdom divides
passages.summary: Rehoboam rejects advice to ease the people’s burden. The northern tribes follow Jeroboam, who establishes worship at Bethel and Dan. Labor grievances and political decisions contribute to division. The calves’ form and function need interpretation beyond assuming every worshiper’s private belief.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies the effect of leaders’ choices and the need for good counsel.

passages.title: A man of God confronts Bethel
passages.summary: A man of God announces judgment at Bethel. An older prophet deceives him into eating, and a lion later kills him. The account combines a future oracle, signs, deception, and death. The older prophet’s claim is explicitly false. The guide does not invent either man’s name.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: Original study reflection: test a claimed revelation without assuming that status makes every claim reliable.

passages.title: Ahijah speaks and Shishak attacks Jerusalem
passages.summary: Jeroboam’s disguised wife visits Ahijah about their son Abijah. The child dies. The account then describes Rehoboam’s rule and Shishak’s attack. Royal households and ordinary people bear consequences in the account. Abijah the child is distinct from Abijam, Rehoboam’s successor.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: Original study reflection: retain the child and grieving household when assessing a royal judgment.

passages.title: Judah’s rulers and a new northern dynasty
passages.summary: Abijam and Asa rule Judah. Asa seeks Ben Hadad’s help against Baasha. Baasha kills Nadab and destroys Jeroboam’s household. The succession notices assess worship and record conflict. The same royal name can refer to different rulers in different generations.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: Original study reflection: compare religious reform with the use of war and purchased alliances.

passages.title: Rapid succession leads to Omri and Ahab
passages.summary: Jehu condemns Baasha’s house. Zimri kills Elah and is defeated. Omri prevails over Tibni, builds Samaria, and is succeeded by Ahab. The narrative records unstable transfers of power. Ahab’s marriage and temple practices lead into the Elijah accounts. Hiel’s sons remain named in the rebuilding notice.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: Original study reflection: consider the human costs of a sequence summarized as royal succession.

passages.title: Elijah and the widow at Zarephath
passages.summary: Elijah announces drought, receives food at Cherith, and stays with a widow at Zarephath. Her food endures, and her son returns to life. The widow expresses scarcity, fear, and grief. Her words matter alongside the prophet’s actions. Cherith’s exact location remains uncertain.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies the widow’s trust amid scarcity.

passages.title: Elijah confronts Ahab at Carmel
passages.summary: Obadiah meets Elijah. At Carmel, Elijah challenges divided allegiance. Fire answers his prayer, the Baal prophets are killed, and rain returns. The narrative connects rain with divine power and includes mass killing. A religious application does not remove that violence from the account.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me uses Elijah’s challenge to examine commitment to God.

passages.title: Elijah receives care and calls Elisha
passages.summary: Threatened by Jezebel, Elijah flees, asks to die, receives food, and travels to Horeb. He receives renewed work and places his mantle on Elisha. Food, rest, and divine communication precede renewed service. The commands to appoint Hazael and Jehu are not reported as completed here.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies the quiet voice and Elisha’s willingness to respond.

passages.title: Ahab defeats Ben Hadad and releases him
passages.summary: Ben Hadad attacks Samaria. Prophets advise Ahab, and Israel wins two battles. Ahab releases his opponent and receives a prophetic rebuke. Military success and divine approval are not identical. The king called Ben Hadad here is kept distinct from Asa’s earlier ally.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: Original study reflection: examine how victory can still leave a leader accountable for a decision.

passages.title: Naboth is killed and Elijah confronts Ahab
passages.summary: Naboth refuses to give up his vineyard. Jezebel arranges false accusations and his killing. Ahab takes possession, and Elijah announces judgment. The king benefits from an injustice carried out through officials and false testimony. Naboth’s refusal concerns inherited land, not simple unwillingness to sell.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: Original study reflection: consider how a person can benefit from wrongdoing arranged by another.

passages.title: Micaiah warns Ahab before the final battle
passages.summary: Ahab and Jehoshaphat seek counsel about Ramoth Gilead. Micaiah describes a heavenly council and predicts defeat. Ahab dies in battle. A large agreement among prophets does not settle the question of truth. The council scene raises difficult questions about deception and divine agency.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: The older manual reads the council as divine permission. This remains an LDS interpretation of a difficult scene.

guides.title: Study 1 Kings
guides.description: Follow selected chapters through the book.

steps.title: Solomon is anointed during a succession dispute
steps.text: Adonijah gathers supporters at En Rogel. Bathsheba and Nathan approach David, who orders Solomon’s anointing at Gihon. Succession depends on public recognition and access to the aging king. Abishag serves David, but the text denies sexual relations.

steps.title: Rehoboam rejects the petition and the kingdom divides
steps.text: Rehoboam rejects advice to ease the people’s burden. The northern tribes follow Jeroboam, who establishes worship at Bethel and Dan. Labor grievances and political decisions contribute to division. The calves’ form and function need interpretation beyond assuming every worshiper’s private belief.

steps.title: Micaiah warns Ahab before the final battle
steps.text: Ahab and Jehoshaphat seek counsel about Ramoth Gilead. Micaiah describes a heavenly council and predicts defeat. Ahab dies in battle. A large agreement among prophets does not settle the question of truth. The council scene raises difficult questions about deception and divine agency.

textRoutes.title: Elijah and the widow at Zarephath
textRoutes.summary: Elijah announces drought, receives food at Cherith, and stays with a widow at Zarephath. Her food endures, and her son returns to life.
textRoutes.detail: The widow expresses scarcity, fear, and grief. Her words matter alongside the prophet’s actions. Cherith’s exact location remains uncertain.

textRoutes.title: Micaiah warns Ahab before the final battle
